name: Deborah

seo.title: Deborah in the Bible: prophetess, judge and her song
seo.description: Deborah in plain words: the prophetess who judged Israel under a palm tree, sent Barak against Sisera, sang the song of Judges 5, and how she is remembered.

band.where: Between Ramah and Bethel, in Ephraim
band.lede: A prophetess who judged Israel under a palm tree. She sent Barak against 900 iron chariots, went with him, and sang the victory.

who: Deborah was a prophetess and a judge of Israel, in the time of the Judges. People came to her for judgment under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. When Jabin of Canaan had oppressed Israel for twenty years, she sent Barak to war and went with him. After the victory they sang the song of Judges 5.

lines: The River Kishon swept them away

numbers.chip: Men who came down Mount Tabor
lines: Barak led; she went with him

numbers.chip: Years of rest after her song

tidbits.text: **Deborah** means **bee**. **Barak** means **lightning**, as Josephus notes, and her husband's name, **Lappidoth**, means **torches**.

cite.text: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 5; Strong's Hebrew 1683, 1301 and 3941, at Bible Hub

tidbits.text: She is the one judge in the book shown hearing cases. The others are judges as “deliverers and leaders”, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.
The Talmud counts seven women as prophets: **Sarah**, **Miriam**, **Deborah**, **Hannah**, **Abigail**, **Huldah** and **Esther**.
Why a palm tree? The rabbis said that, as a woman, she would not judge in private. She judged in the open air, where all could gather.
Her song calls Jael “Most blessed among women”. Elizabeth greets Mary with nearly the same words.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: Under the **Palm of Deborah**, between **Ramah** and **Bethel** in the hill country of **Ephraim**. The Israelites came up to her there for judgment.

facts.label: Husband
facts.text: **Lappidoth**. Judges gives nothing about him but his name.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **prophetess**, who spoke the LORD's word, and a **judge** of Israel, who heard the people's cases.

facts.label: Her enemy
facts.text: **Jabin**, king of Canaan, who reigned in **Hazor**, and **Sisera**, the commander of his army.

facts.label: The battle
facts.text: From **Mount Tabor** down to the **River Kishon**. Her song places it “at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo”.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Debbora**, in older Catholic Bibles and the *Catholic Encyclopedia*.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: Judges does not say. Josephus says that she and Barak died at about the same time.

facts.label: Remembered
facts.text: By the **Orthodox**, on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers in mid-December. No Western church keeps a day for her.

facts.label: In the New Testament
facts.text: Not named. **Hebrews 11** names Barak among the faithful.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Under her palm tree, judging; or singing her song, crowned with laurel, as in the painting at the top. A French engraving of 1647 shows her in armour.

facts.label: Other Deborahs
facts.text: **Rebekah's nurse**, buried under an oak below Bethel (Genesis 35:8), and **Tobit's grandmother**, in the book of Tobit (1:8).

moments.title: The Palm of Deborah
moments.text: After Ehud died, Israel again did evil, and the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. His commander Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron. For twenty years Jabin “harshly oppressed the Israelites”, and they cried out to the LORD. At that time Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel. She would sit under the Palm of Deborah in the hill country of Ephraim, “where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment.”

moments.title: She sends for Barak
moments.text: She summoned Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali, and gave him the LORD's command. He was to take ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun to Mount Tabor. The LORD would draw Sisera, his chariots and his troops to the River Kishon, “and I will deliver him into your hand.”

moments.title: If you go, I will go
moments.text: Barak would not go alone. “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” Deborah agreed at once. But she told him the honour would not be his, for the LORD would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. She went with him, and ten thousand men of Zebulun and Naphtali followed him.

moments.title: Down from Tabor
moments.text: Sisera heard, and brought all nine hundred iron chariots out to the River Kishon. Deborah told Barak that this was the day. He came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men behind him. “And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army.” Sisera left his chariot and ran on foot. Barak chased the army as far as Harosheth-hagoyim, and “not a single man was left.”

moments.title: Into the hand of a woman
moments.text: Sisera ran to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, whose clan was at peace with Jabin. She welcomed him in, gave him milk and covered him with a blanket. As he slept from exhaustion, she drove a tent peg through his temple. When Barak arrived, she showed him the man he was looking for. Deborah's word had come true. “On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites.”

moments.title: The song
moments.text: “On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song”. It fills Judges 5: the LORD marching out from Seir, the tribes who came and the tribes who stayed home, the stars fighting from heaven, Jael's blow, and Sisera's mother waiting at her window. It ends, “And the land had rest for forty years.” More of it follows, in Her song.

extras.title: Her song
extras.lede: Judges tells the victory twice: in prose in chapter 4, and as a song in chapter 5. *Britannica* calls the song “perhaps the oldest section of the Bible”, a glimpse of Israel in the 12th century BC.

items.title: A mother in Israel
items.text: The song looks back on the bad years. The highways were empty, and travellers kept to the byways. Village life had stopped. Then she arose.
items.quote: Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel.

items.title: Who came, and who stayed home
items.text: The song calls the roll. Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali came. Reuben could not make up its mind, Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan, Dan lingered by the ships and Asher by the coast. The town of Meroz is cursed for not coming at all.
items.quote: Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield.

items.title: The stars fought
items.text: The song tells what the prose leaves out. The heavens poured out rain, and the River Kishon swept Sisera's army away. Josephus, writing about 93, tells of a great storm of rain and hail that the wind blew into the Canaanites' faces.
items.quote: From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.

cite.text: Judges 5:4, 20-21; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 5, chapter 5

items.title: Sisera's mother at the window
items.text: The song ends far from the battle, with the enemy's mother. She watches at the lattice for a chariot that will not come. Her wisest ladies tell her he is only late because he is dividing the spoil.
items.quote: Why is his chariot so long in coming? What has delayed the clatter of his chariots?

items.title: Like the sun
items.text: It closes with a prayer. Then Judges adds that the land had rest for forty years.
items.quote: So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.

words.note: Judges records her words in chapter 4. She sang the song of chapter 5 with Barak. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.kicker: At Mount Tabor, the day of battle
feature.q: Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?
feature.ctx: Sisera's nine hundred chariots had come out to the River Kishon, in the valley below.

quotes.q: Surely the LORD, the God of Israel, is commanding you: Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.
the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.

quotes.q: I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.
quotes.who: Near the start of her song, which she sang with Barak.

quotes.q: My heart is with the princes of Israel, with the volunteers among the people. Bless the LORD!

myths.truth: Jael did, in her tent. Deborah foretold only that the LORD would sell Sisera “into the hand of a woman”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* puts it plainly: the prophecy “refers not to Debbora herself, but to Jahel”.

myths.claim: Hebrews 11 names Deborah among the heroes of faith.
myths.truth: It names Barak: “Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets”. Samuel's farewell speech names Barak too. No other book of the Bible names her.

circle.name: Barak
circle.text: Son of Abinoam, from Kedesh in Naphtali. He led the ten thousand down Mount Tabor, but only with her beside him. Hebrews 11 names him among the faithful.

circle.name: Lappidoth
circle.text: Her husband. Judges gives only his name. A later rabbinic story makes him Barak himself.

circle.name: Jael
circle.text: The wife of Heber the Kenite. Sisera fled to her tent, and she killed him there. The song calls her “most blessed of tent-dwelling women.”

circle.name: Sisera
circle.text: The commander of Jabin's army, from Harosheth-hagoyim. He fled the battle on foot and died in Jael's tent. Psalm 83 still prays, “Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon”.

circle.name: Jabin
circle.text: King of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor and oppressed Israel for twenty years. After the battle the Israelites' hand “grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him.”

saint.big: The Orthodox honour her as **Righteous Deborah**, on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers. No Catholic or Protestant calendar keeps a day for her.

churches.note: Sunday of the Holy Forefathers, 11 to 17 December
Not in the Mass calendar or the 1916 Martyrology
The ELCA names her in a prayer for the saints

paras: The OCA lists **Righteous Deborah** among those remembered on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers. It falls between 11 and 17 December, so she has a Sunday rather than a date. Her whole entry sends the reader to Scripture: “Information about the holy Prophetess and Judge Deborah may be found in the Book of Judges 4:5-14, and also chapter 5.”

Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, has no day for her, and nor does the calendar used at Mass today. The Church of England, the Episcopal Church and the Missouri Synod Lutherans keep none either.
The ELCA's book *Evangelical Lutheran Worship* (2006) names her, with Gideon, in its prayer of thanks for the saints of old.

kin.name: Hannah
kin.text: Her prayer became a song of victory: “My heart rejoices in the LORD.” The Talmud counts both women among Israel's seven prophetesses.

kin.name: Judith
kin.text: Another woman who saved Israel and led its song of thanks. John Chrysostom named the two together.

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: She saved her people at the risk of her own life: “And if I perish, I perish!” The Talmud names her among the seven prophetesses too.
